analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to intimidate election officials and workers, including by displaying firearms near them.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote after being introduced in the final weeks of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new section to the Voting Rights Act making it illegal to intimidate, threaten, or coerce anyone carrying out federal election duties — counting votes, tabulating, canvassing, or certifying results — or anyone targeted because they used to hold such a job. It would also create a legal presumption in civil suits that someone visibly carrying a firearm while interacting with voters or election workers is engaging in intimidation, rebuttable if they show otherwise, with an exception for on-duty law enforcement [S2]. The bill was introduced on September 25, 2024 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Election administrators, poll workers, and vote counters — many of them temporary or volunteer workers — who have faced threats and harassment during and after elections, and voters who want election results counted without interference [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal prohibition on intimidating, threatening, or coercing anyone exercising powers or duties to administer federal elections, including vote counting, tabulation, canvassing, and certification, and protects former election workers targeted for their past role [S2].

Establishes a rebuttable presumption that visibly displaying or carrying a firearm while interacting with voters or election workers violates the Voting Rights Act's anti-intimidation provisions, easing the burden of proving intimidation in civil suits [S2].
Allows courts to grant relief including reasonable temporary limits on defendants' carrying of firearms, and exempts on-duty law enforcement officers from the presumption [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People who carry visible firearms near polling places and election offices could face civil enforcement, and gun-rights groups object that the presumption burdens lawful carry; taxpayers fund enforcement through the Justice Department.
analysis.who_pays_short: Visible gun carriers near election sites

drawbacks.text: The firearm presumption shifts the burden: a person visibly carrying a gun near a polling place is presumed to have committed intimidation unless they prove otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence, which open-carry advocates view as too broad a restriction on lawful behavior near elections [S2].

Existing federal law already prohibits voter intimidation and threats against federal officials, so critics could argue the new provisions overlap with current protections rather than filling a gap [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target a real and documented problem — threats against election workers — and the firearm presumption is rebuttable with an on-duty police exception, which softens the civil-liberties objection. The main cost falls on the small set of people who visibly carry guns around election sites, and the enforcement mechanism is civil, not automatic criminal prosecution. A fair trade for most readers, though the burden-shifting presumption is the most contestable feature.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Deluzio introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, with eight Democratic cosponsors, in the final weeks of the 118th Congress [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the bill's action history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Election workers gain nothing from the bill's death, since no protection was enacted; the status quo — with intimidation left to existing, narrower laws — is unchanged. No industry or interest was materially at stake, so the main 'winner' is simply anyone who preferred no new limits on visible firearms near election sites.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; no new protections enacted

for.name: Rep. Chris Deluzio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled eight Democratic cosponsors in the final weeks of the Congress.

for.name: Reps. Ruiz, Connolly, Grijalva, Goldman, Lee, Carbajal, Garcia, and Norton
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with the chamber's schedule controlled by the majority, an unmarked-up bill could not advance.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported it, and the Republican-controlled committee and floor never acted on it [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would create a presumption that visible firearms near voters or election workers constitute unlawful intimidation, restricting armed presence at election sites. The impact is limited to civil enforcement and excludes on-duty police.

industries.industry: Local election administration (county clerks, poll workers)
industries.note: The bill would give election workers a federal cause of action against intimidation and threats, a workforce that is largely low-paid or volunteer. The bill died before any of this took effect.
